overview: This two-document file records a September 1947 inquiry and the Department of State’s October response concerning the mailing of parcels to occupied Japan. It covers parcel frequency, weight and dimensional limits, acceptable noncommercial relief goods, duty and customs-clearance treatment, prohibited valuables, merchandise samples and commercial papers, restrictions on printed matter and tobacco, and the requirement that addresses written in Chinese or Korean also be given in Roman characters. The routing and distribution stamps show the question circulating among several Department of State offices concerned with occupied areas and Northeast Asian affairs.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-742 requesting information on parcels to Japan
subfiles.about: The airgram requests guidance on sending parcels, particularly foodstuffs, to Japan and on applicable size or quantity limitations.
subfiles.summary: This brief incoming airgram poses two questions about shipments to Japan. It asks what kinds of articles, including foodstuffs, may be sent and requests information about dimensional or quantitative restrictions. Departmental stamps show that the inquiry circulated through offices handling American republic, occupied-area, and Northeast Asian affairs before being filed on October 22, 1947.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply on postal shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State; Robert A. Lovett, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Unidentified U.S. diplomatic post that sent airgram A-742
subfiles.about: The Department explains the rules governing relief parcels and other mailed articles sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Responding to airgram A-742, the Department describes limits on parcel frequency, weight, dimensions, and contents, emphasizing noncommercial relief goods for an addressee and immediate family. It identifies acceptable medicines, clothing, and relief articles; imposes quantitative restrictions on saccharine and tobacco; prohibits such valuables as pens, watches, and cameras; and explains the disposition of undeliverable parcels. The reply also discusses duty-free treatment, customs-clearance charges, merchandise samples and commercial papers, restrictions on books and periodicals, and the need to interline Chinese- or Korean-language addresses in Roman characters.

interest: The file offers a compact but unusually concrete view of the practical regulation of private relief shipments to Japan during the early postwar occupation. Its detailed distinctions among family relief, commercial samples, written materials, tobacco, valuables, and printed matter are useful for studying material scarcity, customs administration, and transnational aid. The Roman-character requirement also documents how language and script affected postal administration, while the numerous routing stamps reveal the Department of State bureaucracy through which such operational questions passed.
